newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds follow sell-off and slip.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds follow sell-off and slip.

text.p: Irish bonds slipped back in moderate late afternoon trade on Wednesday in line with a sell-off on bond markets around the globe, dealers said.

"Bonds were marked up this morning in a positive reaction to the FOMC decision to leave interest rates alone," a dealer said. "But conditions have become much slippier this afternoon -- perhaps the market suspects that inflationary pressures are still ahead and is pricing in the long-end risk."

The Federal Reserve's decision yesterday to leave interest rates steady initially gave the market heart, but some analysts take the view that the Fed will be forced to raise rates by half a point at the next FOMC meeting in early July.
By 1510 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 22 pence at 102.05 to yield 5.94 percent while the key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 35.5 pence at 109.13 to yield 6.64 percent.

There was a bias to sell on the Irish market, the dealer said, additionally influenced by a bout of domestic punt-selling and by the backdrop of a weaker-than-expected response to Tuesday's NTMA auction of long-dated paper.
"We've seen curve flattening today and this is largely due to a slight tightening of money-market rates which pushed up short-end bond yields," the dealer said.
Dealers said the spreads on Irish bonds over Germany were broadly unchanged from the close, trading at 141 basis points above in the five-year area, and 78 above in the 10-year area.
